title: Deposition scheduling calls: capture constraints without interpreting the notice
audience: court reporting and litigation support firms
request: an attorney, assistant, witness, or videographer wants to schedule or change a deposition
fields: requesting firm, case reference, witness name as provided, proposed dates and timezone, remote or in-person format, venue, estimated duration, services requested, accessibility request, and secure callback details
boundary: interpreting a subpoena, deciding whether notice is sufficient, giving legal advice, promising reporter availability, or sharing case information before verification
scenario: A legal assistant requests a next-morning remote deposition and says the notice will follow. The receptionist records the requested services and timing but does not call the matter confirmed or assess whether notice is valid.
source_name: U.S. Courts Federal Rules of Civil Procedure resources

title: Commercial laundry service calls: identify downtime and machine risk before dispatch
request: a hotel, care facility, or laundromat reports a washer or dryer failure
fields: site and callback, machine asset number, make and model if visible, observed display code, cycle stage, water or heat condition, unusual sound or smell, shutdown status as reported, access hours, and operational impact
boundary: telling staff to open guarded equipment, diagnose electrical or gas faults, bypass an interlock, promise a part, or estimate safe return to service
owner: the commercial equipment dispatcher or qualified technician
scenario: A care facility reports a dryer stopped mid-cycle and staff noticed a hot smell. The receptionist captures the direct observations, applies the approved safety escalation, and avoids reset instructions.

title: Septic emergency calls: distinguish backup hazards from routine pumping requests
audience: septic pumping and onsite wastewater service companies
request: a caller reports sewage backup, surfacing wastewater, an alarm, odor, or an overdue tank pumping
fields: service address, caller location, affected fixtures or outdoor area, observed wastewater, alarm wording, time first noticed, occupancy, nearby well or surface water as reported, access constraints, and callback number
boundary: telling a caller to enter a tank, open a lid, handle sewage, diagnose system failure, guarantee an arrival time, or declare the property safe
scenario: A homeowner reports wastewater at a basement floor drain after heavy rain. The receptionist records the affected area and observations, follows the company's hazard script, and does not recommend opening the tank.

title: Standby generator calls: route test failures and outages without remote troubleshooting
audience: generator maintenance and electrical service contractors
request: a standby generator fails a test, alarms, runs unexpectedly, or does not start during an outage
fields: service address, generator asset reference, fuel type if known, display wording, whether utility power is out, observed sound or odor, load status as reported, people relying on powered equipment, prior service, and safe callback number
boundary: instructing an untrained caller to open panels, handle fuel, bypass a transfer switch, diagnose a fault, or promise that critical equipment is protected
owner: the electrical service dispatcher or licensed on-call technician
scenario: A clinic reports an outage while its generator display shows a fault and the unit is silent. The receptionist records the exact display and critical-load concern, escalates immediately, and gives no panel-reset instructions.

title: Hearing-aid repair calls: separate device logistics from clinical questions
audience: audiology practices and hearing-aid service centers
request: a patient reports a lost, damaged, intermittent, or nonworking hearing aid
fields: patient and callback, device side, brand and model if known, serial or service reference through the approved channel, observed problem, loss or damage date, warranty record status, communication preference, and appointment constraints
boundary: diagnosing hearing change, recommending medical treatment, deciding warranty coverage, requesting unnecessary health details, or promising a same-day repair
owner: the audiology service coordinator or licensed clinician
scenario: A patient says the right device stopped working after getting wet and also reports sudden hearing difficulty. The receptionist separates the device repair request from the symptom escalation and routes each to its approved owner.

title: Emergency glass and board-up calls: capture exposure, occupancy, and access facts
audience: commercial glass and emergency board-up contractors
request: a caller reports a broken storefront, window, door glass, or unsecured opening
fields: exact address, opening location and approximate size, cause as reported, loose or hanging glass, injuries or immediate danger reported, occupancy, weather exposure, security contact status, site access, photos through the approved channel, and callback number
boundary: telling anyone to handle broken glass, enter an unsafe area, certify structural safety, promise police response, or guarantee a board-up time
scenario: A restaurant manager reports a shattered front door after closing, with glass still in the frame. The receptionist confirms the opening and access contact, follows the emergency script, and does not tell staff to clear the glass.

title: Irrigation leak calls: collect zone and property facts without unsafe shutoff advice
request: a property contact reports continuous watering, pooling, a broken head, low pressure, or suspected irrigation-line damage
fields: property address, leak location, zone if known, observed flow, start time, controller status as reported, street or building impact, recent work, available access, account reference, and callback number
boundary: directing excavation, telling a caller to enter a flooded area, diagnosing a main-line break, operating unfamiliar valves remotely, or promising water savings or repair scope
scenario: An apartment manager reports water crossing a sidewalk from a landscaped area while no scheduled cycle is running. The receptionist records the observation and pedestrian impact, then escalates under the approved leak policy.

title: Access-control service calls: restore routing without exposing security details
audience: commercial door and access-control service providers
request: a verified property contact reports a door, reader, lock, credential, or access-control panel failure
fields: verified account and caller role, service address, affected entrance described without sensitive codes, failure behavior, occupancy impact, life-safety concern reported, event time, approved onsite contact, technician access method, and callback number
boundary: collecting passcodes in notes, revealing security configuration, instructing a bypass, disabling a life-safety device, or promising that a site is secure
owner: the authorized access-control dispatcher or security technician
scenario: A facility manager reports that employee badges fail at one staff entrance while the door remains locked. The receptionist verifies the account, avoids recording credentials, and routes the operational impact to the security queue.

title: Medical-waste pickup calls: record container and incident facts without handling advice
audience: regulated medical-waste transport and service companies
request: a clinic requests pickup, reports a missed service, or raises a container, spill, or storage concern
fields: verified account and site, waste stream named by the caller, container type and count, pickup reference, storage area, observed damage or release, people exposed as reported, facility incident lead, access window, and callback number
boundary: classifying unknown material, telling staff to handle a spill, accepting prohibited items, changing manifests, or stating regulatory compliance on the phone
owner: the medical-waste operations or compliance coordinator
scenario: A dental office reports a sharps container arrived damaged but says no material is visible outside it. The receptionist records only observations, invokes the provider's incident path, and gives no repacking instruction.

title: Portable restroom service calls: capture placement, access, and sanitation priorities
audience: portable sanitation rental and service companies
request: an event organizer or jobsite contact requests delivery, relocation, cleaning, restocking, or urgent service
fields: account and site, unit identifiers and count, requested service, event or shift timing, placement surface, truck access, locked-gate contact, accessibility needs, observed sanitation issue, and callback number
boundary: promising code compliance, directing unsafe relocation, guaranteeing a delivery window, accepting hazardous material, or marking service complete before route confirmation
owner: the route coordinator or field-service dispatcher
scenario: A festival contact reports two units are unusable before gates open and asks that they be moved across soft ground. The receptionist separates sanitation urgency from placement feasibility and routes both to operations.

title: Property survey scheduling calls: prepare access and document facts for the surveyor
request: an owner, buyer, lender, attorney, or contractor asks for a boundary, location, construction, or elevation survey
fields: requesting party and role, property address and parcel reference, requested survey purpose in the caller's words, transaction or project deadline, known access restrictions, occupants, documents available, delivery contact, and callback number
boundary: interpreting a deed, locating a boundary by phone, quoting a legal conclusion, promising completion before record review, or treating an estimate as authorization
owner: the survey project coordinator or licensed surveyor
scenario: A buyer asks whether a fence is on the lot line and needs an answer before closing. The receptionist records the decision needed and deadline but does not interpret the fence location or promise a survey result.
source_name: Bureau of Land Management cadastral survey resources

title: Commercial refrigeration alarms: route temperature facts without food-safety decisions
request: a restaurant, grocer, pharmacy, or warehouse reports a temperature alarm or cooling failure
fields: site and callback, equipment or case identifier, displayed temperature and unit, time observed, setpoint if visible, alarm wording, product type described generally, door and power status as reported, backup storage status, and prior service reference
boundary: declaring food or medicine safe, directing disposal, diagnosing refrigerant or electrical faults, telling staff to open equipment, or guaranteeing restoration time
owner: the refrigeration dispatcher or qualified on-call technician
scenario: A market manager reports a walk-in display at 48°F for an unknown duration while other cases appear normal. The receptionist timestamps the reading, records the affected unit, and leaves product disposition to the authorized business owner.
